knowledge_point.title: Writing First-Order Linear ODEs in Standard Form

question.:question/problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
2 \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} + 5 \cos{(x )}=7 y \sin{(x )} - 3\,.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}2 \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} + 5 \cos{(x )}=7 y \sin{(x )} - 3 \\ 2 \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} - 7 y \sin{(x )}=- 5 \cos{(x )} - 3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\underbrace{(- \frac{7 \sin{(x )}}{2})}_{P(x)}y=\underbrace{- \frac{5 \cos{(x )}}{2} - \frac{3}{2}}_{Q(x)}\end{gathered}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=- \frac{7 \sin{(x )}}{2}$ and $Q(x)=- \frac{5 \cos{(x )}}{2} - \frac{3}{2}.$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{- 5 x + 7 y}{x}\,.
$$

Assume $x\ne 0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{- 5 x + 7 y}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{- 5 x}{x}+\frac{7 y}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} - \frac{7 y}{x}=\frac{- 5 x}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\underbrace{(- \frac{7}{x})}_{P(x)}y=\underbrace{-5}_{Q(x)}\end{gathered}

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=- \frac{7}{x}$ and $Q(x)=-5.$

\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} - 8 y \cot{(x )} - 2 \sin{(2 x )}=0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} - 8 y \cot{(x )}=2 \sin{(2 x )} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\underbrace{(- 8 \cot{(x )})}_{P(x)}y=\underbrace{2 \sin{(2 x )}}_{Q(x)}\end{gathered}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=- 8 \cot{(x )}$ and $Q(x)=2 \sin{(2 x )}.$
